detailed_analysis:
The fit is excellent overall: global R2 = 0.9967, peak_region_r2 = 0.9939, well above the 0.90 acceptance gate, with residual_rms/noise = 2.6 (acceptable given very high peak counts) and no unmodelled-reflection spikes remaining after the retry added components at ~15.5, ~28.7, and ~43.4 deg. Forty reflections are resolved across 10-45 deg, the density of low-angle peaks confirming a large-unit-cell hybrid/molecular phase as expected for an imidazolium tetrachloroaurate system.

FWHMs cluster in the 0.10-0.45 deg range, which per the domain size table corresponds to typical microcrystalline-to-nanocrystalline material (roughly 20-50 nm). Applying Scherrer per peak yields lower-bound sizes spanning ~16 nm (broad low-angle lines, e.g. peaks 1, 7, 32) up to ~50-78 nm for the narrowest lines (peaks 8, 16, 18). This >3x spread across peaks is a domain-flagged inconsistency: it points to anisotropic broadening (anisotropic crystallite shape or hkl-dependent strain) and/or peak overlap in the fitting windows, so an isotropic single-number Scherrer size would be an oversimplification. The correct report is a size RANGE (~16-78 nm, with the bulk of well-isolated peaks in the ~25-40 nm band), not a mean. A Williamson-Hall analysis is warranted before any size/strain decomposition; I would not report W-H numbers until its linearity R2 is checked (>=0.9 needed for confident decomposition, and a negative slope would indicate background/calibration/misassignment problems).

The eta values are bimodal and mostly pinned at the bounds (many ~1e-9 = near-pure Gaussian, a few ~0.4-1.0 = strongly Lorentzian). Per the validation rules, eta pinned at 0/1 typically means the data do not constrain the mixing for those (often weaker or overlapped) peaks; the size numbers derived from their FWHM inherit this uncertainty and should carry the standard +/-15% (or larger) accuracy caveat.

Crucially, this is a single frame of an in-situ thermal ramp (31->120 C, 1 K/min). Under the sample-and-mounting priors, a variable-temperature run is exactly the case where the lattice genuinely moves - so peak-center shifts frame-to-frame are the physical signal of interest (thermal expansion, and potentially a phase transition / precursor decomposition en route to metallic Au or an intermediate). The refined centers here are the anchor for tracking that evolution. No phase has yet been assigned; structure matching is the natural next step. The apex misfit at 11.6 deg is accepted as the profile limit and does not affect these conclusions.

scientific_claims.claim: The precursor phase at this ramp temperature is microcrystalline-to-nanocrystalline with an anisotropic coherent domain size, with per-reflection Scherrer sizes spanning ~16-78 nm (most well-isolated peaks ~25-40 nm, FWHM ~0.10-0.45 deg), rather than a single isotropic size (+/-15% typical accuracy, and larger where eta is unconstrained).
scientific_claims.scientific_impact: Establishes that the imidazolium tetrachloroaurate precursor crystallizes as anisotropic domains, which controls how the crystallites reorganize and decompose during the thermal ramp toward gold-containing products; the >3x per-peak size spread signals anisotropic morphology or hkl-dependent strain that a naive single-size report would hide.
scientific_claims.has_anyone_question: Has anyone observed anisotropic (hkl-dependent) crystallite-size broadening in imidazolium tetrachloroaurate precursors, and does the anisotropy evolve during in-situ thermal ramps?

model_type: Sum of split (asymmetric) pseudo-Voigt peaks on SNIP background (global fit_pattern, auto-detected peaks, 10-45 deg)

verification_iterations.model: Sum of split (asymmetric) pseudo-Voigt profiles, one per detected Bragg reflection, on a SNIP-estimated background. Each pseudo-Voigt: amplitude, center (2θ), FWHM, and Gaussian/Lorentzian mixing eta in [0,1]. Number of components set by auto-detection (expect ~25–35 significant reflections across the range); the intense low-angle peaks (~11.55, ~13.0, ~14.75, ~16.4, ~22.15, ~23.05°) and the resolved higher-angle peaks are all real reflections to be modelled.

issues.problem: A clear data maximum near x≈28.7 is entirely unmodelled; the fit passes as a smooth ramp beneath a distinct broad reflection.
A resolved data peak near x≈43.4 is not fit; the model runs monotonically through it.
A shoulder/small maximum near x≈15.5 between the two strong peaks is under-resolved.

verification_iterations.fix_applied: Re-run fit_pattern with max_peaks raised above 30 and prominence_frac lowered (e.g. ~0.01) so auto-detect adds components at x≈28.7, x≈43.4, and x≈15.5; the model type stays split_pseudo_voigt.

verification_iterations.model: Sum of split (asymmetric) pseudo-Voigt profiles, one per detected Bragg reflection, on a SNIP-estimated background. Each pseudo-Voigt has amplitude (>0), center (2θ), FWHM in [0.05°, 2.0°], and Gaussian/Lorentzian mixing eta in [0,1]. The reflection set now explicitly includes the previously missed features: a broad reflection at 2θ≈28.7°, a resolved peak at 2θ≈43.4°, and a weak shoulder at 2θ≈15.5° between the strong ~14.75° and ~16.4° peaks. Together with the intense low-angle peaks (~11.55, ~13.0, ~14.75, ~16.4, ~22.15, ~23.05°) and resolved higher-angle peaks, the component count is expected to rise above ~30 (now ~28–38 significant reflections across 10–45°). Model type remains split_pseudo_voigt (LOCKED).

issues.problem: A broad low-intensity data feature (a shallow plateau/hump between the sharp lines) is under-resolved; the fit runs as a smooth ramp beneath the diffuse intensity.
Slight asymmetry/apex misfit on the tallest reflection produces a coherent residual lobe on the high-angle flank.
